note_claims.claim: Patient has had vomiting and diarrhoea since last week.
Patient has had about five non-bilious, milky vomits since last night, with fewer today.
Patient has had six to seven loose stools today.
There is no blood in the patient's stools.
The patient's brother had blood in his stool with a similar illness last week.
The patient has had two wet nappies since this morning.
The patient is taking small amounts of breast milk and formula.
Patient's temperature is 37.4 °C.
Patient is alert and playing.
Patient is not drowsy or floppy.
Patient has no rash.
Patient is previously well.
Patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
Mucous membranes are moist.
Anterior fontanelle is not sunken.
Probable viral gastroenteritis with reduced urine output.
Continue breastfeeding.
Administer oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) in small, frequent amounts.
Call 999 if the patient becomes floppy, very sleepy, or hard to wake.
Attend A&E if the vomit goes green or if blood is seen in the nappy.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician is calling Freya's mother.
The relative is Leanne.
Clinician is Dr Mistry calling back from the surgery.
The relative is holding Freya on her lap.
The clinician asks to confirm Freya's date of birth.
Freya's date of birth is the Fourteenth of December.
Freya is ten months old.
Freya started being sick last night and has diarrhoea this morning.
Clinician asks how many times Freya has been sick.
Freya has been sick about five times since last night, and less today.
Clinician asks what colour the vomit is and if it is ever green.
The vomit is milky, and it is just her milk coming back.
Clinician asks how many dirty nappies there are.
There are six or seven runny dirty nappies today.
Clinician asks if there is any blood in the nappies.
There is no blood in Freya's nappies, but her brother had blood in his stool with a similar illness last week.
Clinician asks if her brother had a similar illness.
Freya's brother got the illness at nursery, and Freya goes to the same nursery.
Clinician asks about wet nappies today.
The relative initially thought there were about four wet nappies, but corrected this to only two wet ones since this morning, noting the others were dirty.
Clinician confirms there are two wet nappies since this morning and asks if she is drinking.
Freya is having little bits of milk and is breastfed and has a bit of formula.
Clinician asks if she has had a temperature.
Freya's temperature was 37.4 this morning.
Clinician asks how she is in herself and if she is alert or playing.
Freya is grumpy but is watching the telly and playing with her blocks.
Clinician asks if she is very sleepy, floppy, or hard to wake.
The relative confirms she is not very sleepy or floppy.
Clinician asks about a rash.
The relative reports no rash.
Clinician asks about medical problems, medicines, and allergies.
The relative states there are no medical problems, medicines, or allergies.
Clinician suggests the condition is likely gastroenteritis, possibly the same one her brother had, and that most babies get better within a few days.
Clinician expresses concern about the low number of wet nappies and requests a face-to-face review at four o'clock.
The relative agrees to the review at four o'clock.
Clinician advises continuing to breastfeed and giving small amounts of oral rehydration solution (like Dioralyte) every few minutes.
The relative agrees to the advice.
Clinician provides safety netting advice: call 999 if the patient becomes floppy, very sleepy, or hard to wake, or if a rash does not fade when pressed with a glass.
The relative acknowledges the safety netting advice.
Clinician advises taking the patient to A&E if the vomit goes green or if blood is seen in the nappy.
The relative agrees to the safety netting advice and confirms the appointment time.
